I've been playing around recently with a less appreciated explanation of the Fermi Paradox. It comes up every now and then as a throwaway line in a paper or blog post, but you rarely see anyone give it much airtime. I have some ideas about why that might be, and why the epistemic ground is shifting.

The Fermi Paradox (FP) [@Sandberg2018], also known as the Great Silence [@Brin1983], asks why, given the fact that life can evolve and apparently alters its environment in highly conspicuous ways, do we see no evidence of it elsewhere in the galaxy. [It gets harder and harder to understand as we detect more planets in habitable zones [@Bryson2021].]{.lc-param data-param="N"}

Back in the 60s when Frank Drake famously made a start on related calculations, he thought about detecting life as hearing their radio signals [@Drake1961]. Some contemporaries were already expecting life to make more noise than that, most famously [Freeman Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyson_sphere) [@Dyson1960]. This view didn't become central to the field until the 70s, but nowadays people who work on FP expect life to [move beyond its starting planet and dim its star]{.lc-param data-param="q"}, and spread to neighboring stars and do the same [@Hanson2021; @OlsonOrd2021]. Whether we have any right to expect this, from where we are sitting today, is a good question and one of the first objections often raised against this kind of work. One of the results that fell out of my calculations, completely unexpectedly, was a way to put a numerical value on this objection-- and the objection is strong. I will give that objection its own section, alongside all other objections of the form 'how would we know, what would we see, what would make us confident in an observation'.

But first, let me get to the model and its assumptions.

# 1. The Lineage

At conception an egg fuses with a sperm cell and starts the miracle of ontogenesis. That egg was formed early in the development of the mother, while she was in the womb, going through her own ontogenesis, from her own egg, which was inside her mother. And on and on, through many as-yet poorly understood evolutionary leaps and bounds back to LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. Take note of one simple thing here-- the egg never dies. The cell never dies. Individual cells can die, individual lineages can be cut. But the egg from which you grew was the descendant of an unbroken lineage of simple cells, multiplying and reproducing, back deep into pre-history. Until when exactly? That is the question, and we can pick two bounds quickly. The Earth formed about [4.6 billion years ago (4.6 Gya)]{.lc-param data-param="T first"} and the Big Bang happened around 13.8 Gya.

The first bound, the origin of the Earth, is taken as the default hypothesis. The statement 'after the Earth cooled and liquid water appeared in large quantities life evolved and reached the level of bacteria by 3.7Gya, possibly earlier' [@Nutman2016] could be a summary of the most common position. @Moody2024 used phylogenetic analysis to date LUCA at 4.2 Gya.

There is an unbroken lineage of cells going back for around 4 billion years. The reason this lineage is unbroken is that counterfactual lineages that form spontaneously out of nothing have not been observed. The miracle of life earns its epithet-- it is a remarkably improbable phenomenon. LUCA is estimated to have had 2.5 million base pairs. The greatest unanswered question in evolutionary theory is, how did something so complex emerge spontaneously on the early Earth so quickly?

My preferred answer is that it simply didn't. The lineage didn't start on Earth, it came from outer space. This is known as panspermia, the seeding of life on planets through meteors or other means [@Kawaguchi2020; @AdamsNapier2022]. Panspermia strikes a lot of people as wacky at first glance, because it invites the first mover question. Who sent the seeds, some alien civilization? In which case, per the above, why don't we see any other evidence of them? But the version I follow is not so exotic. It is simply that the accumulation of enough chemical complexity for hereditary ecosystems to kick-start must have taken billions of years, and could have happened anywhere with the right combination of starting materials and temperature, pressure, and energy flow. The pre-Earth part of the story is long, boring, and spread out across the galaxy in a vast number of pockets, large and small [@SharovGordon2013].

# 2. The Start

How does this help with the Fermi Paradox? Surely the fact that life's precursors were around before Earth and are presumably relatively common in the universe should mean we would see more life, everywhere, not less of it? That is true, and is one of the testable differences between the long lineage and the hard steps model. But more on that later.

The main problem the hard steps model solves is that, if life evolved on one planet from a standing start, it could have done so on earlier planets. 75% of the planets in the galaxy are older than ours, many by billions of years [@Lineweaver2004]. Anything expanding from one of those planets would have had enough time by now to take over and transform the entire galaxy. The hard steps model solves this by making life on any given planet exceedingly unlikely. Indeed, it has to be so unlikely that there would only be [one surviving lineage every *million galaxies*]{.lc-param data-param="lambda"} [@Hanson2021]. 

It's worth dwelling for a moment on this value, $\lambda = qN$. It combines the number of lineages in the galaxy with their probability of expansion. In the left, there are sliders for q and N, but under the default settings they are incompatible-- hence we also show $\lambda$, the combined number that is forced by the empty sky.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 1 · How long did the lineage take?]{.lc-figure-title}

```{ojs}
{
  const lam = p.q * p.N;
  const Ts = d3.range(0.5, 13.55, 0.25).map(t => { const c = LC.planetCeiling(p, t); return {x: t, y: isFinite(c) ? Math.min(c, 1e12) : NaN}; });
  const yMin = 10 ** Math.floor(Math.log10(Math.min(...Ts.map(d => d.y).filter(isFinite), lam, 1e-12))), yMax = 1e12;
  return chart({
    width: 680, data: Ts, ylog: true, xdom: [0.5, 13.5], ydom: [yMin, yMax],
    xticks: [1, 4.6, 8, 12], yticks: decTicks(yMin, yMax, Math.log10(yMax / yMin) > 16 ? 6 : 4),
    yfmt: t => pow10(Math.log10(t)), xtitle: "time to emerge T (Gyr)", ytitle: "largest qN an empty sky allows",
    color: "var(--planet)", forbid: "above", markers: [{x: p.T, y: lam, label: "your qN", left: p.T > 9}],
    tip: d => `T ${d.x.toFixed(2)} Gyr · qN ≤ ${sci(d.y)}`
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const lam = p.q * p.N, ceil = LC.planetCeiling(p, p.T), lead = LC.T0 - LC.S - p.T;
  const head = `Each planet starts the lineage at its own birth and needs time <i>T</i> to emerge. Planets have been forming since 0.2 Gyr, so at <i>T</i> = ${p.T.toFixed(1)} Gyr the first emergences came ${dur(lead)} before ours. The curve is the most loud lineages per galaxy, Λ = <i>qN</i>, that leave the sky empty`;
  if (!isFinite(ceil)) return caption(`${head}; at this <i>T</i> nothing is ruled out, even with every lineage loud.`);
  const fits = lam <= ceil;
  const tension = fits
    ? `Your sliders give <i>qN</i> = ${sci(lam)}, under the curve, so the sky stays empty.`
    : `Your sliders give <i>qN</i> = ${sci(lam)}, ${sci(lam / ceil)} times too many: the sky would be full of loud galaxies. <i>q</i> and <i>N</i> cannot both stand. Keep <i>N</i> = ${sci(p.N)} lineages per galaxy and almost none may expand, <i>q</i> ≤ ${sci(ceil / p.N)}. Keep every lineage loud and lineages must be rare: one per ${sci(1 / ceil)} galaxies.`;
  return caption(`${head}: at this <i>T</i>, Λ ≤ ${sci(ceil)}. ${tension} Push <i>T</i> towards the age of the universe and the ceiling lifts.`);
}
```

:::

By contrast, if it simply takes life much longer than the lifetime of the planet to get started, the fact that we are emerging now is not so remarkable. In this view, we are emerging now and apparently alone because we are essentially synchronized with all other lineages.

Here the other bound comes in, the lifetime of the universe. If you work through the geometric calculation, as Hanson does in the grabby aliens model [@Hanson2021], you realize that we must be synchronized not only within our galaxy, but also between galaxies. If there is such a thing as a galaxy-transforming civilization, [the light from its distant now-transformed galaxy would have reached us by now]{.lc-param data-param="lead"}.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 2 · The head-start cap]{.lc-figure-title}

```{ojs}
    xtitle: "loud lineages per galaxy, qN", ytitle: "largest head start δ", color: "var(--shared)", forbid: "above",
    markers: [{x: Math.min(Math.max(lam, 1e-4), 1e8), y: 1000 * lead.delta, label: "your qN", left: lam > 1e5}],

```

```{ojs}
{
  const lam = p.q * p.N, lead = LC.sharedLead(p, "visibility", p.W), arr = LC.sharedLead(p, "arrival", p.W);
  const rad = LC.C * Math.max(lead.delta - LC.HOST_MPC / (p.v * LC.C), 0), gal = 4 / 3 * Math.PI * p.ng * rad ** 3;
  const saturated = lam >= 10;
  let text = `Now let progress carry between planets from one shared start. Every lineage in a galaxy emerges on the same date, so planet age stops mattering; what matters is how far ahead of ours the first galaxy's date sits. The curve is the largest head start δ an empty sky allows. `;
  if (p.W === 0) {
    text += lead.capped
      ? `With your <i>qN</i> = ${sci(lam)}, δ ≤ ${dur(lead.delta)}. A lead δ exposes loud galaxies out to about <i>c</i>δ: here a sphere of ${rad < 100 ? rad.toFixed(1) : sci(rad)} Mpc holding about ${sci(gal)} galaxies. ${saturated ? "Every galaxy in it is loud, so more lineages per galaxy change nothing: the plateau." : "Few lineages turn loud, so a longer lead hides behind the rarity."} Fronts arriving here, rather than light, would allow ${arr.capped ? dur(arr.delta) : "any lead"}.`
      : `With your <i>qN</i> = ${sci(lam)}, loud galaxies are rare enough that no lead within the 13.6 Gyr history is ruled out.`;
  } else {
    text += lead.capped
      ? `Spread the starts over a window of ${dur(p.W)} and the first galaxy can lead by up to ${dur(lead.delta)}, but only if our own start lies in the window's first ${pct(lead.delta / p.W)}. A wider window buys a longer lead and pays for it with a position nearer the front.`
      : `With starts spread over ${dur(p.W)}, the sky never binds: we can sit anywhere in the window.`;
  }
  return caption(text);
}
```
:::


What could synchronize the start of different lineages across such enormous scales? It has to be something very early. There are a few candidates, such as the habitable epoch in the early universe, the so-called goldilocks epoch around 17 million years after the Big Bang [@Loeb2014]. However there was nothing at that time capable of retaining information, no carbon to form structure. The first carbon showed up [between 100 and 200 million years in]{.lc-param data-param="W"} [@Bromm2013; @StacyBromm2014], and that is the time that I have chosen to start my clock. That is the time when structure started to form, when the first rocky bodies started to form (the first stars went supernova in only a few million years, so there would have been rocky bodies forming throughout that era).

Another thing that draws me there is the remarkable coincidence between the age of Earth and the age of the universe. We could plausibly have woken up on a planet orbiting a red dwarf a trillion years from now. Then we would have good reason to be surprised by the empty sky! But our planet is about 1/3 the age of the entire universe. Jumping from 4 billion years of evolution to 13 billion years of evolution is, from a certain perspective, quite a small step.

# 3. The Race

Extending the history of our evolutionary lineage to the start of the universe is simple enough, and does help limit the population of the sky. But surely over the last 13 billion years there must be some variance in the speed of evolution. This is true, and we can make some guesses about how much that might be, or at least model different estimates. If, for example, we allow the speed of evolution to [vary by 1%]{.lc-param data-param="sigma"} [@Hair2011] and we believe there is one lineage per habitable planet, and we suppose that we have evolved at an average speed, then there would be 30 other lineages emerging from their planets per year right now in this galaxy, and there would already have been 5 billion lineages that emerged over the last 850 million years.

In this example, the typical lineage is still [about a billion years from emerging]{.lc-param data-param="typical"}. We belong to a thin first wave, arriving around now in galaxy after galaxy.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 3 · Durations that vary: the first flush]{.lc-figure-title}

```{ojs}
flush = LC.durationSpread({N, q, v, ng, pEmpty}, sigma)
```

```{ojs}
{
  const r = flush;
  if (!r) return html`<div></div>`;
  const span = r.meanAfter + 2 * p.sigma, back = Math.min(3 * p.sigma, LC.T0 - LC.S);
  const fLo = 10 ** (Math.floor(Math.log10(r.F)) - 3);
  const data = d3.range(121).map(i => { const x = -back + (span + back) * i / 120, F = LC.phi(x / p.sigma - r.z0); return {x, y: F < fLo ? NaN : F}; });
  return chart({
    width: 680, data, ylog: true, xdom: [-back, span], ydom: [fLo, 1],
    xticks: niceTicks(-back, span), yticks: decTicks(fLo, 1, 3),
    xfmt: t => t === 0 ? "today" : (t > 0 ? "+" : "−") + dur(Math.abs(t)), yfmt: t => pow10(Math.log10(t)),
    xtitle: "time from today", ytitle: "share of lineages emerged", color: "var(--shared)",
    refs: [{y: 1 / p.N, label: "one lineage in a galaxy"}, {y: 0.5, label: "half emerged"}],
    markers: [{x: 0, y: r.F, label: "today"}, {x: r.meanAfter, y: 0.5}],
    tip: d => `${d.x >= 0 ? "+" : "−"}${dur(Math.abs(d.x))} · ${sci(d.y)} emerged`
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const r = flush;
  if (!r) return caption(`With these inputs the sky stays empty even with the typical lineage emerging today, so the sky sets no limit.`);
  return caption(`Give each lineage its own duration, drawn independently with a spread of ${dur(p.sigma)} (${(100 * p.sigma / 13.6).toPrecision(2)}% of 13.6 Gyr). The fastest of ${sci(p.N)} draws per galaxy lands far ahead of the typical one, and an empty sky forbids those early runners from having turned loud. So the typical lineage has to sit in the future: ${dur(r.meanAfter)} from now. By today only ${sci(r.F)} of lineages have emerged, which leaves an expected ${sci(r.home)} loud lineages ahead of us in the Milky Way, and a ${pct(r.pFirst)} chance we are the first. ${isFinite(r.wait) ? `The first front from another galaxy reaches us in about ${dur(r.wait)}.` : ""} All of this rests on the far left tail of the duration law, where nothing physical pins the shape: a hard minimum duration would allow no early runners at all.`);
}
```
:::

The number of emerging lineages in this result is of the order of N, the total number of lineages in our model. These are the aliens we are racing against. The fact that the sky is empty means we can't have been sitting around-- we can't be in the middle of the pack, or we would see the evidence of the leaders all around us. If you picture us as a random lineage, the chance of being this far ahead is about [one in a hundred billion]{.lc-param data-param="rank"} — roughly one over the number of lineages.

I'll talk about luck more below, but it's worth thinking about the rest of the players in the race. To make the model simple, I have chosen to assume that there is one evolutionary lineage per habitable planet. But that wraps a lot of assumptions up into one. First, we don't really know what that means, and we are changing our model of it all the time. Some people are stricter about what constitutes a goldilocks zone, some say a planet needs a moon and a nice stable star. And perhaps the seeds, perhaps LUCA, is not so common that every planet gets seeded at exactly the right moment, or other planets are more prone to destabilizing catastrophes than ours. The number of other lineages N, that is, the number of our contemporaries, the number of our competitors in the race for the front, varies a lot model to model.

Changing the number of competitors changes our luckiness and the number of contemporaries we would expect to meet in our galaxy, but several other parts of the models are insensitive to it, such as [the number of lineages ahead of us in our galaxy]{.lc-param data-param="ahead"} and the spread in time. The empty sky still needs an explanation, even if there are only a hundred or less surviving lineages per galaxy.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 4 · The sky fixes the count, not the share]{.lc-figure-title}

At <i>N</i> = ${sci(p.N)} we are 1 in ${sci(1 / F)}, with ${sci(p.N * F)} ahead of us. Across nine decades of <i>N</i> the rank moves almost as 1/<i>N</i> while the count ahead barely moves. # 4. Luckiness

However fondly you may think of our lineage, however proud you may be of the cyanobacteria that transformed the atmosphere or the plucky archaea that first swallowed up a prokaryote and formed our domain, we do still seem to have been the beneficiaries of some remarkable rolls of the dice. Every model of the Fermi Paradox has to do it-- to guesstimate our luck. Let's start with that, and then think about ways we might make it a little firmer.

There are two broad ways to portion out the luck. The first is the hard-steps lottery, going back to Brandon Carter [@Carter1983; @Watson2008; @SnyderBeattie2021], which models evolution as [a series of improbable events]{.lc-param data-param="n hw"}, events that normally don't happen in any given lineage-- the origin of life, eukaryotes, sex, multicellularity, language, etc. [@MaynardSmithSzathmary1995] These transitions are modelled as inherently unlikely, so unlikely that any given planet might not pass even one of them. A planet such as ours has passed through a series of major flukes to get where it is today.

Hard steps was built to explain a coincidence on Earth: we turned up fairly late in the Sun's habitable lifetime, which is what you'd expect if the path here ran through several long shots. It has since become the standard way to keep the sky empty. But a recent review by Mills and colleagues [@Mills2025] argues that the case for any particular step being hard is weak. Several of the 'steps' waited on the planet changing, not on biological luck, and when you look closely each one breaks down into smaller pieces that each pay their way. Take language for example. Vocal cords evolve because communication of any sort over distance is beneficial to a community of genetically related individuals. Memory benefits any organism that has to interact with a sometime-predictable world. As memory develops, an organism can learn things within a lifetime that might benefit its offspring or cousins, so more advanced forms of communication and instincts for copying evolve. All the parts of advanced language are beneficial individually, and it's easy to understand how it could have progressed, becoming more and more powerful as it evolves. 

To my eye, the hard-steps lottery looks like it's backfilled into the data once the uncompromising geometry of our situation is recognized. But the only thing that forces it is the assumption that life began on Earth, which gives other planets billions of years of head-start. If you drop that assumption, the starting clock seems more intuitive.

And the luck backs it up. The frame I use for the calculation is called Full Non-Indexical Conditioning [@Neal2006], and it asks what is the chance of finding an observer in a given situation. For the hard-steps model, what are the odds that there is a lineage on a planet observing an empty sky after having passed through such and such of a number of hard steps after evolving there for 4 billion years. For the process clock model, what are the odds that there is a lineage on a planet observing an empty sky after having evolved for 13 billion years.

There are two ways to count luck here. The first is personal: what are the odds that our lineage, out of all of them, ended up this far ahead? That depends heavily on how many lineages there are. With a million lineages in our galaxy, the process clock needs us to be about one in 30 million. The hard-steps lottery needs us to be about one in ten trillion. Change the number of lineages and both numbers move, but the hard-steps one is always about a million times worse.

The second is the one that matters for choosing between theories: how often does a universe like this produce anyone in our position, emerging now under an empty sky? That one barely cares how many lineages there are, and here the process clock beats hard steps by a factor of [ten million to a billion]{.lc-param data-param="fnc"}. The reason is timing. The process clock bunches its arrivals into a wave a few tens of millions of years wide, so it only has to keep the sky quiet for that long. The lottery spreads them over billions of years, so it has to keep them rare the whole time.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 5 · Two ways to count luck]{.lc-figure-title}

:::

With regard to the process clock, you might be tempted to make our situation less unlikely by changing the number N. Indeed, you could imagine a synthesis of the hard-steps and process models, along the lines of 'life is very unlikely, takes a great deal of environmental fortune, and so there are only a handful of surviving lineages per galaxy'. In this scenario we are not particularly lucky at all, it is simply the case that life takes 13 billion years to evolve, and there are only a handful of habitable zones in the galaxy that have happened to be seeded by the right stuff at the right time. There is something quite pleasant and parsimonious about this. And it feels like it takes on the important conceptual lessons from the hard-steps model-- let's not throw out the baby with the bathwater.

On the other hand, someone has to be first, and it might as well be us. Probability can help us select between competing hypotheses, but it can't stop us from looking out at the empty sky and finding ourselves surprised. I would rather think that N is high, there are many lineages out there, and we will meet them someday than believe that the galaxy is essentially barren.

But there is one last thing that has to be contended with. We must deal with doom.

# 5. The Filter

In 2010, Katja Grace informed us that [the filter is ahead](https://meteuphoric.com/2010/03/23/sia-doomsday-the-filter-is-ahead/) [@Grace2010SIA]. That is to say, when observing an empty sky, the chances are you will not live to colonize it.

With our default scenario, an observer like us is [about a billion times more likely]{.lc-param data-param="doom"} in a world with a hard filter than without, and for the hard-steps model it's about a million billion or more.

This value essentially prices all the standard objections to the model. The typical late filter framing imagines that building Dyson spheres is the default outcome, and some catastrophe must stop us from going through with it. However there are many scenarios that should be combined here. In *Diaspora* [@Egan1997], Greg Egan has a society of artificial entities set out on a galactic mission in a ship the size of a grain of rice. The 'doom tax' really covers all of these scenarios-- not only the probability that we won't ever blot out the sun due to catastrophe, but also the probability that we will simply choose not to, or find a more efficient way to run society, or escape into a pocket dimension where we will enjoy unlimited energy and resources forever. By reflection, it also models the chance that there are already other advanced civilizations, that are simply invisible to us or unrecognizable.

This was the biggest surprise that fell out of the model, for me. The fact that the most common intuitive objections to this entire enterprise show up, here, at the end, when we try to work out our luck.

But one more thing is worth mentioning. I said earlier that our luck really tracks the number of other lineages in our galaxy. If we are the only one, we don't have to be so lucky. Well, the doom tax, the idea that our situation is likelier if there is a great filter coming up, also tracks N. And it therefore gives us an easy way out of it-- just suppose we are alone in the galaxy, and the doom shrinks from a billion to a factor of 20.

::: {.lc-figure}
[Figure 6 · The doom tax]{.lc-figure-title}

```{ojs}
doomSweep = {
  return d3.range(1, 11.01, 0.5).map(l => {
    const r = LC.observerRates({...sky, N: 10 ** l}, sky.sigma, {n: settledN, W: settledHw, z0s: [3, 0]});
    return {x: 10 ** l, lo: r.process.filter[0].obs / r.process.loud.obs, hi: r.process.filter[1].obs / r.process.loud.obs,
            lottery: r.lottery.filter.obs / r.lottery.loud.obs};
  });
}
```

:::

This is convenient, but to me it is unsatisfying. I would rather attack the doom tax with better priors. If we take it as a measure of our uncertainty that we will build a Dyson sphere we can point at Starlink and say, look, we are already launching solar-powered infrastructure into space in significant quantities. We only need to keep to the exponential for a century and we're there. In this framing, I might excuse myself for watching the Starship launches so avidly, as each one constitutes a Bayesian update against great filter doom.

# Conclusion

I entirely credit Sharov and Gordon's *Life Before Earth* [@SharovGordon2013] with inspiring this work. I had heard about panspermia before, read it in some Hanson blogs, in some science fiction stories. But Life Before Earth really jarred me and changed the way I thought about evolutionary history. In the years since, other sources fed into this frame of mind, Chaisson's ERD papers [@Chaisson2011], England's dissipative adaptation [@England2015], and most recently Assembly Theory [@Sharma2023Assembly]. Hanson's Grabby Aliens model [@Hanson2021] inspired me to take the empty sky seriously as an observation, and think about what you could derive from there.

While I was working on this intensely in the last couple of weeks, one of my searches turned up @Ponfilenok2026, an independent researcher who uploaded a remarkably similar preprint just a couple of months ago, drawing inspiration from all the same sources as me. His model and his aims are slightly different from mine, and his scholarship is more thorough, so I happily acknowledge his precedence. It will take me a while to fully digest his paper, but I will try to write a note detailing exactly where we differ and by how much. More interesting though is where he has gone further into the possible mechanism and the thermodynamics.

The premise of this work is quite simple, take a few observations and assumptions and grind them through the machinery of statistics until something comes out the other end. But really, the reason ideas like this come around is because of all the mass of circumstantial and partial glancing lines of reasoning and evidence that push you towards them. All the things that you can't fit into the model. All the lines of evidence that relate to this topic are getting richer and making progress all the time. Every asteroid we touch, every other planet we probe and sample, every distant star system or galaxy we observe adds evidence and allows us to sharpen up the numbers one way or another.

Indeed, research into evolutionary history, molecular biology, sociology on Earth can also often be folded into it. This is the real fun of Fermi thinking. Understanding the evolution of complex life folds in all our endeavours, and speaks to each of them.

*Per Ardua, ad Astra*.

See you, space cowboy.


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## What the calculation assumes

- **Trajectories, not planets.** *N* counts effective retained-progress trajectories per galaxy in Earth-equivalent units: 10¹¹ stars × 0.1. It grows linearly from cosmic age 0.2 Gyr to today, 13.8 Gyr. Trajectories are never destroyed.
- **Turning loud.** A lineage that crosses the threshold turns loud with probability *q*. It then spreads through its galaxy (30 kpc) and keeps spreading at speed *v*. The results mostly depend on Λ = *qN*.
- **Seeing it, or meeting it.** A galaxy is visible once its front has crossed it and the light has reached us. Arrival means the front itself reaching us. Each galaxy is independent, so P(empty) = e^−μ^.
- **The sky.** Loud fronts spread at 0.5*c*. Galaxies sit at 0.01 per cubic megaparsec. The sky counts as empty while it has at least a 5% chance of showing no loud galaxy, which means about three expected. All three can be changed under *The sky* in the sidebar.
- **Geometry.** Space is flat with a fixed galaxy density. That is fair for the few megaparsecs behind the 14 Myr cap. Over the gigaparsecs the planet clock integrates, treat it as a scaling statement.
- **What it does not do.** It does not derive the shared clock from chemistry, model survey completeness, or turn percentiles into odds for our own existence.

The numbers on this page are recomputed in your browser by a port of the repository's Python model and match the note's tables. Full write-up: *First-flush likelihood under a common-start, continuous evolutionary process* ([PDF](https://github.com/FergusFettes/lineage-cap/blob/main/first-flush-likelihood.pdf), [code and data](https://github.com/FergusFettes/lineage-cap), [doi:10.5281/zenodo.23406424](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23406424)). Text CC BY 4.0, code MIT.
:::

```{ojs}
//| output: false
// Shared state for every figure.  Each slider lives once in its home figure; copies elsewhere
// are bound to it, so moving any copy moves them all.  The model is site/model.js.
import {makeSlider, toggle, caption, paramPanel, resultRows, card, verdict, row, sci, pow10, dur, pct, oneIn, niceTicks, decTicks} from "./widgets.js"
Plot = import("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@observablehq/plot@0.6.16/+esm")
LC = window.LineageCap
B = LC.BASELINE
views = ({
  N: makeSlider("N", B.N), q: makeSlider("q", B.q), v: makeSlider("v", B.v), ng: makeSlider("ng", B.ng),
  pEmpty: makeSlider("pEmpty", B.pEmpty), T: makeSlider("T", B.T), W: makeSlider("W", B.W),
  sigma: makeSlider("sigma", B.sigma), n: makeSlider("n", 6),
  hw: toggle({label: "Lottery planets stay habitable", value: Infinity, options: [["for ever", Infinity], ["for 5 Gyr", 5]],
    help: "Whether a hard-steps planet can only emerge within a 5 Gyr habitable window."})
})
N = Generators.input(views.N)
q = Generators.input(views.q)
v = Generators.input(views.v)
ng = Generators.input(views.ng)
pEmpty = Generators.input(views.pEmpty)
T = Generators.input(views.T)
W = Generators.input(views.W)
sigma = Generators.input(views.sigma)
nSteps = Generators.input(views.n)
lotteryWindow = Generators.input(views.hw)
p = ({N, q, v, ng, pEmpty, T, W, sigma})
// Heavy sweeps follow a slider only when it is released, so dragging stays smooth.
settled = view => Generators.observe(notify => {
  const f = () => notify(view.value);
  notify(view.value);
  view.addEventListener("change", f);
  return () => view.removeEventListener("change", f);
})
sky = ({v: settledV, ng: settledNg, pEmpty: settledPEmpty, sigma: settledSigma, q: 1, N: 1})
settledV = settled(views.v)
settledNg = settled(views.ng)
settledPEmpty = settled(views.pEmpty)
settledSigma = settled(views.sigma)
settledN = settled(views.n)
settledHw = settled(views.hw)
panel = paramPanel(views, numbers, ["v", "ng", "pEmpty"])
numbers = resultRows([
  {title: "If every planet starts its own clock", items: [["first", "First emergences, before ours"], ["lambda", "Loud lineages per galaxy (qN), at most"], ["qn", "Your qN"]]},
  {title: "If all lineages share one start", items: [["lead", "Largest head start over us"]]},
  {title: "If durations vary between lineages", items: [["typical", "Typical lineage emerges in"], ["rank", "Our rank among lineages"], ["ahead", "Loud lineages ahead of us at home"]]},
  {title: "Shared start against hard steps", items: [["fnc", "Observers like us, shared start over hard steps"], ["doom", "Doom tax: how much likelier a late filter makes us"]]}
])
{
  const lead = LC.T0 - LC.S - p.T, ceil = LC.planetCeiling(p, p.T), shared = LC.sharedLead(p, "visibility", p.W);
  const r = flush;
  const tax = R.process.filter.map(f => f.obs / R.process.loud.obs);
  numbers.set({
    first: lead > 0.0005 ? dur(lead) : "none",
    lambda: isFinite(ceil) ? `≤ ${sci(ceil)}` : "no limit",
    qn: {text: sci(p.q * p.N), ok: !(p.q * p.N > ceil)},
    lead: shared.capped ? `≤ ${dur(shared.delta)}` : "unbounded",
    typical: r ? dur(r.meanAfter) : "–",
    rank: r ? oneIn(r.F) : "–",
    ahead: r ? sci(r.home) : "–",
    fnc: `× ${sci(R.process.loud.obs / R.lottery.loud.obs)}`,
    doom: `× ${sci(Math.min(...tax), 1)}–${sci(Math.max(...tax), 1)}`
  });
  void panel;
}
// A line chart in the old site's style: log axes optional, an excluded region, markers, hover tip.
chart = (o) => Plot.plot({
  width: o.width || 460, height: 260, marginLeft: 58, marginBottom: 40, style: {background: "transparent"},
  x: {type: o.xlog ? "log" : "linear", domain: o.xdom, ticks: o.xticks, tickFormat: o.xfmt, label: o.xtitle, labelAnchor: "center", labelArrow: "none"},
  y: {type: o.ylog ? "log" : "linear", domain: o.ydom, ticks: o.yticks, tickFormat: o.yfmt, label: o.ytitle, labelArrow: "none", clamp: true, grid: true},
  marks: [
    o.forbid ? Plot.areaY(o.data.filter(d => isFinite(d.y)), {x: "x", y1: "y", y2: o.forbid === "above" ? o.ydom[1] : o.ydom[0], fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.07}) : null,
    o.forbid ? Plot.text(["excluded"], {frameAnchor: o.forbid === "above" ? "top-left" : "bottom-right", dx: 8, dy: 8, fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.6}) : null,
    ...(o.refs || []).map(r => [Plot.ruleY([r.y], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4, strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
      Plot.text([r.label], {x: o.xdom[0], y: r.y, dx: 6, dy: -7, textAnchor: "start", fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.7})]),
    Plot.lineY(o.data.filter(d => isFinite(d.y)), {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: o.color, strokeWidth: 2.2}),
    Plot.dot((o.markers || []).filter(m => isFinite(m.y)), {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5.5, fill: o.color, stroke: "var(--card)", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.text((o.markers || []).filter(m => isFinite(m.y) && m.label && !m.left), {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", dx: 9, dy: -9, textAnchor: "start", fontWeight: 600, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.text((o.markers || []).filter(m => isFinite(m.y) && m.label && m.left), {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", dx: -9, dy: -9, textAnchor: "end", fontWeight: 600, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleX(o.data.filter(d => isFinite(d.y)), Plot.pointerX({x: "x", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.3})),
    Plot.tip(o.data.filter(d => isFinite(d.y)), Plot.pointerX({x: "x", y: "y", title: o.tip}))
  ]
})
```
